bridges.description: Whether testimony for Jesus’s miracles can make those extraordinary events believable.
The comparative evidential threshold imposed by violations of ordinary natural expectations.
Whether the transmission, memory, and authorship of the Gospel reports support historical confidence.
Whether analogous miracle traditions weaken a special inference to Christian miracle claims.
Whether resurrection and salvation claims belong to publicly checkable historical knowledge or faith commitment.
Whether the formal historical case makes Jesus’s miracles credible enough to believe.
Whether early witnesses had informed first-person access rather than merely sincere inherited belief.
Whether early sources, named Gospel transmission, and ordinary historical accuracy support the miracle reports.
Whether hostile and non-Christian testimony corroborates the claimed public reputation for miraculous acts.
Whether rival miracle traditions lack the early, close, costly, and multiply attested features claimed for Jesus.

sections.title: Probability, testimony, and the threshold for miracles
sections.rationale: The motion turns first on what evidence could make an extraordinary miracle report believable and how competing explanations should be compared.

sections.title: Historical sources, authorship, and memory
sections.rationale: Both sides directly contest whether ordinary accuracy, Gospel identity, eyewitness investigation, and memory support the miracle inferences.

sections.title: Witness sincerity, access, and martyrdom
sections.rationale: A central dispute is whether costly commitment supplies only sincerity or also informed access to the alleged events.

sections.title: Competing miracle traditions and hostile testimony
sections.rationale: Both sides test the Christian claims against other religious traditions and against purportedly hostile or independent testimony.

sections.title: Mythology, historical meaning, and closing epistemology
sections.rationale: The remaining dispute concerns mythic parallels and the closing distinction between historical evidence, experiential meaning, and faith commitment.
